text.title: AI rout deepens: Nasdaq falls 5.3%, Nvidia plunges and S&P 500 and Dow close in correction
text.summary: US stocks sold off sharply on Friday as the AI trade unwound. The S&P 500 fell 3.7% for a seventh straight loss, the Nasdaq dropped 5.3% and the Dow slid 1.9%. Technology was the epicenter, with the sector ETF down 7.3%, and the VIX jumped 26.2% to 35.9. Treasuries rallied, with the 10-year yield down 14 bp to 4.91%, but the usual havens did not all hold: gold fell 4.1% and Bitcoin fell 5.0%. The dollar was flat and oil rose 1.3% but is still down for the week. The common thread is a loss of confidence in the AI spending boom, which spread from mega-cap tech into the broader market.
text.rates: The 10-year yield closed at 4.91%, down 14 bp, and the 2-year at 4.63%, down 13 bp. Both have fallen over the past five days as money moved into Treasuries. The dollar index was flat at 103.88. Oil rose 1.3% to $83.54 but is down 5.7% on the week, its third straight weekly loss, as global supply conditions improved. Gold fell 4.1% to $3,534, so neither bonds nor the dollar fully absorbed the equity stress and the pressure showed up across asset classes.
text.breadth: The selling was broad but concentrated in growth. Technology fell 7.3%, industrials 3.1%, consumer discretionary 3.0%, communication services 2.7% and materials 2.2%. Consumer staples rose 0.7% and health care was nearly flat at -0.1%, so investors leaned defensive. The Russell 2000 fell 2.8% and the Dow fell 1.9%, both less than the S&P 500's 3.7% and the Nasdaq's 5.3%, because the AI selloff hit the biggest growth names hardest. Canadian stocks also entered a correction.
text.context: The S&P 500 has fallen seven straight sessions and is 10.9% below its one-month high, down 8.6% over five days. J.P. Morgan's weekly recap showed the S&P 500 up 11.5% year to date and the Nasdaq up 8.7% as of Nov 13, and the Nasdaq has now erased its 2026 gain. J.P. Morgan put the S&P 500 at 18.2x forward earnings as of that date, before this week's decline. The VIX is up 86% over five days.
text.takeaway: Sharp, concentrated drawdowns in a market's leading theme are a normal feature of long-term investing, and they show why diversification across sectors and asset classes matters. The day also showed that correlations can rise in stress, so no asset class offered a guaranteed shelter.
text.talk: The market had a sharp selloff driven by doubts about the AI spending boom, with Nvidia and tech hit hardest and volatility spiking. Treasury yields fell and defensive sectors held up better, and it's a reminder to stay focused on long-term plans and diversification.

drivers.t: Anthropic's public debut was meant to validate the AI buildout, but the stock slid after its first session and has stayed only above its IPO price. CNBC reported that the decline weighed on the broader market as the S&P 500 and Dow closed in correction. WSJ framed the week as a $4 trillion AI wipeout. A weak debut for the sector's flagship listing tends to challenge the valuations and funding assumptions behind other AI names. MarketWatch also flagged billions of locked-up Anthropic shares that could add supply later. Bloomberg Economics' Anna Wong argued Anthropic's market position has narrowed.
drivers.impact: AI sentiment cracks, Nasdaq erases 2026 gain

drivers.t: Nvidia fell 14% and logged its longest weekly losing streak since 2008, and is now the third-largest US company behind Apple and Microsoft. The stock has shed $1.16 trillion in market value over seven sessions, and one fund manager says uncertainty leaves it vulnerable to more selling. Reuters reported that Nvidia's accounting is a focus of an SEC investigation, citing sources. Nvidia's heavy index weight means its fall pulls the cap-weighted benchmarks down with it. The Technology sector ETF fell 7.3% and the Nasdaq fell 5.3%, turning negative for the year.

President Trump vowed to stop US companies from building data centers abroad and threatened a 'tremendous tax,' after a summit with Xi and Putin in China. MarketWatch noted that the stock market kept falling despite the threat, so this was not a policy scare that markets could look through. Penalties on overseas capacity would add uncertainty to the cost of AI infrastructure, which is already the market's central worry. The headlines do not say how much of today's move this caused.

drivers.h: Volatility spikes, selling feeds on itself
drivers.t: The VIX closed at 35.9, its highest since the April 2025 tariff turmoil, as the S&P 500 posted its worst week in seven months. Goldman's traders said their panic gauge neared its maximum and signaled another substantial wave of selling over the coming week. Schwab's Liz Ann Sonders said relative calm in the major indexes had hidden widespread losses underneath. Rising volatility typically forces risk-managed funds to cut exposure, which can amplify declines. Gold's 4.1% drop and Bitcoin's 5.0% drop fit a pattern of broad de-risking, though the headlines don't explain them directly.

Treasury yields fell sharply as stocks sank. The 10-year dropped 14 bp to 4.91% and the 2-year dropped 13 bp to 4.63%, with WSJ noting that yields plunged. Falling yields reflect demand for safer assets and a lower discount rate for future earnings, which would normally cushion growth stocks. That support was overwhelmed by the earnings and valuation doubts around AI names. The 10-year is now 24 bp lower over five days.

Bloomberg reported that CrowdStrike is in talks to acquire Zscaler in one of the largest-ever cybersecurity deals. Zscaler jumped 18% on the report. Takeover premiums can lift a target even in a falling market, and CNBC noted that security firms have been hunting for acquisitions in the AI era. It was a rare bright spot in a tech sector that fell 7.3% overall.
